CAUSAL MODELING · FINAL PROJECT

Do coupons create sales, or just give money away?

Estimating the causal effect of targeted coupon campaigns from two years of purchases by 2,500 households

Data: dunnhumby “The Complete Journey”

What did the coupons buy?

Customers may use a coupon on milk they would buy anyway. The real question is unobservable: what would the same household have spent without it?

THE CAUSAL GRAPH

Who influences whom

Past shopping drives both who gets a coupon and how much a household spends.

Orange arrows are the backdoor paths.

A coupon can only be redeemed if it was received.

Dashed boxes are things we cannot observe.

T: coupon campaign. H: pre-campaign shopping history. R: redemption. Y: spending. U, V: unobserved.

READING THE GRAPH

Adjust for shopping history, never for redemption

FORK

T ← H → Y

Past shopping causes both the coupon and the spending

Confounding. Block it by adjusting for H.

CHAIN

T → R → Y

Redemption carries part of any effect

A mediator. Leave it alone.

COLLIDER

T → R ← V

Redeemers are households that shopped more that week

Conditioning on R opens a false path.

Backdoor criterion: pre-campaign history blocks every backdoor path, and the campaign cannot have changed it.

T: coupon campaign. H: pre-campaign shopping history. R: redemption. V: shopping in the campaign weeks. Y: spending.

THE RESULT

+1%

Weekly spending after a campaign: no detectable lift

95% confidence interval −8% to +11%, which includes zero. Baseline spending $46.3 a week; change +$0.59.

No effect was detected, and a lift above about 11% can be ruled out. That is not proof that the effect is zero.

COMPARISON

Without adjustment, the estimate slides early

Subtract one line from the other to get the effect in each week. Blue, the weighted estimate, hovers around zero.

Orange is the unadjusted estimate: it slides before anyone has a coupon.

That is regression to the mean, so a simple before/after comparison cannot be trusted here.

Effect on weekly spending ($). Band: 95% confidence interval from 1,000 household-level bootstrap draws.

A SECOND OPINION

Fifteen estimators, one placebo test, same answer

Each method runs twice: on the campaign weeks, and on the 8 weeks before, where the true effect is zero.

Nine pass the placebo. Their answer: −$0.1 to +$1.3 a week.

Propensity-score weighting misses the placebo by $8.

ANCOVA, propensity scores four ways, S/T/X-learners, double ML, doubly robust learner, causal forest. Raw gap: +$26.

A TEMPTING MISTAKE

“Customers who used a coupon spent more”

+$7.5

8 weeks before
no coupons yet

+$7.8

During the
campaign

Extra weekly spending of later redeemers vs controls

Many marketing reports compare coupon users with non-users. Done that way, households that redeemed spend about $8 a week more during the campaign.

But before the campaign started, they were already spending $7.5 more.

Redemption is a collider: it depends on the coupon and on how much the household shops that week. Splitting on it treats an outcome as a cause, so we compare by who received coupons.

266 first-time recipients that later redeemed, against the weighted control group.

WHO RESPONDS

No type of household shows a clear response

A causal forest estimates an effect for every recipient household.

Every group’s interval includes zero.

Estimates rise slightly with shopping frequency, from +$0.3 to +$1.3 a week, and the intervals all overlap.

Recipients in four equal groups by trips per week before the campaign. Intervals as reported by EconML.

THE LIMITS OF THIS DATA

A 1% lift needs about 72,000 households per group

Lift to detectHouseholds per group
10%718
5%2,872
2%17,951
1%71,805

A household spends $46 a week on average, but the change from before to after has a standard deviation of $31. With that much noise, small effects need very large samples.

This study has 1,033 treated households and can reliably detect effects of about 14% or more.

Yet redemptions can have generated at most 0.4% of spending directly.

Randomized test, 5% significance, 80% power. 0.4% assumes every redeemed item was purely incremental.

WHAT TO DO NEXT

The experiment that would settle it

STEP 1

Take the campaign’s normal target list

STEP 2

Sort it into four tiers by shopping frequency

Blocking

STEP 3

Within each tier, hold out a random 10%

Randomization

STEP 4

Compare spending, adjusting for spending before

ANCOVA

Random assignment leaves no backdoor path to block. Blocking and ANCOVA cut the sample for a 1% lift from 135,000 to 58,000 households per group.

A 2% lift with a 10% holdout needs about 81,000 households in total. 5% significance, 80% power.

CONCLUSION

Coupons mostly subsidized existing purchases

Coupons went to the most loyal customers, most were never used, and those that were used went on things they already buy.

RECOMMENDATIONS

Four recommendations for the retailer

01

Hold out a random control group

Leave 5–10% of targeted households without coupons, at random, and measure the lift directly.

02

Rethink who gets coupons

Send some to customers whose shopping is middling or falling: a coupon can still change them.

03

Rethink which coupons to send

Only a coupon for a category not yet bought can create a new purchase: 6% of redemptions today.

04

Judge by incremental sales

A high redemption rate says coupons were used, not that they brought in new spending.

APPENDIX

Method and limitations

SAMPLE

The first 16 weeks are a data ramp-up. Outcomes use weeks 17–101; the 2,269 households present by week 16 are kept.

TREATED AND CONTROLS

Five cohorts receiving a large campaign for the first time: 1,033 households. Controls have no campaign by week 12 after the start.

WEIGHTING

Entropy balancing matches controls to the treated on spending, trips and visit frequency in four pre-campaign periods (12 measures).

ESTIMATOR

Doubly robust: weighting, then regression adjustment. Regression alone gives +1.8%; weighting alone +1.3%.

CONFIDENCE INTERVALS

Household-level bootstrap, 1,000 replications, redoing the weighting and regression each time.

LIMITATIONS

Not a randomized experiment. It assumes households with the same pre-campaign records would have followed the same path without coupons. The check window supports this but cannot prove it.

The full analysis is in coupon_causal_analysis.ipynb and runs end to end from the raw data.

APPENDIX

Why propensity-score weighting fails here

Median chance of receiving the campaign: 0.54 for recipients, 0.02 for the rest.

After weighting, the controls count for only about 190 households.

A few rows carry most of the weight, and baseline spending stays unbalanced.

Propensity score from a logistic regression on the 12 pre-campaign measures and cohort.

Letting the data draw the graph

A Bayesian network learned by hill climbing with the BIC score.

It keeps no arrow from Coupon to Spend.

High spenders: 66% with a coupon, 28% without. Once habits are fixed: 75% and 75%.

Five variables in three levels each. Only arrows that run against time were forbidden.

APPENDIX

An instrumental-variable view

Did not redeemRedeemed
No mailing (Z = 0)6,1260
Mailing (Z = 1)914119

Like the Google ad test: the mailing is the assignment, redeeming is the take-up. Nobody redeems without a mailing, and 11.5% of recipients redeem.

Effect per redeeming household: +$5 a week, with an interval from −$30 to +$45.

Dividing by a small take-up rate multiplies the uncertainty by nine. And the mailing is not a valid instrument: it was targeted, and it may work as a reminder without any coupon being used.

Effect of the mailing (+$0.59 a week) divided by the share of first-time recipients who redeem within 12 weeks.

The retailer re-selects households for each campaign from their recent shopping, which an earlier campaign may have changed.

Shopping in between is a confounder for the second campaign and a mediator for the first.

The g-formula models it under each treatment history. No contrast can be told apart from zero.
